facts.statement: Ikanogavialis had an extremely elongated snout that made up more than 80% of its skull length.
facts.quote: Ikanogavialis possessed an extremely elongated snout accounting for more than 80% of the skull length

facts.statement: Ikanogavialis had very numerous teeth oriented horizontally, resembling a sawfish, with 30 on each maxilla and 31 on each dentary.
facts.quote: The teeth were very numerous (30 on each maxillae, and 31 on each dentary) and they were oriented horizontally, superficially resembling a sawfish.

facts.statement: The type species I. gameroi was named in 1970 based on fossils found in the Urumaco Formation of Venezuela.
facts.quote: The type species of Ikanogavialis is I. gameroi. It was named in 1970 from material found from the Urumaco formation of Venezuela, South America.

facts.statement: Fossils of Ikanogavialis have been found in the Urumaco Formation in Urumaco, Venezuela.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in the Urumaco Formation in Urumaco, Venezuela.

facts.statement: The strata containing Ikanogavialis remains are late Miocene in age, correcting earlier beliefs that they were Pliocene.
facts.quote: The strata from which remains are found are late Miocene in age, rather than Pliocene as was once thought.

facts.statement: Ikanogavialis likely lived in a coastal paleoenvironment alongside other gavialids like Gryposuchus.
facts.quote: Ikanogavialis may have lived in a coastal paleoenvironment along with other gavialids such as Gryposuchus.

facts.statement: Ikanogavialis is classified within the subfamily Gryposuchinae.

It is debated whether the Pleistocene gavialoid from Woodlark Island, Papua New Guinea, belongs to Ikanogavialis, as it was originally named Gavialis papuensis in 1905 but the poor fossil quality makes determination difficult.
facts.quote: Additionally, a Pleistocene gavialoid found on Woodlark Island of Papua New Guinea was initially named Gavialis papuensis in 1905, but has since been proposed to be a member of Ikanogavialis, although the poor quality of the preserved material makes it difficult to determine.

facts.statement: The proposal to refer the Pleistocene form Gavialis papuensis to Ikanogavialis is not widely accepted.
A 2007 phylogenetic analysis placed Ikanogavialis within the subfamily Gryposuchinae alongside genera such as Aktiogavialis, Gryposuchus, Piscogavialis, and Siquisiquesuchus.
facts.quote: A phylogenetic analysis conducted in a 2007 study found Gryposuchinae to include the genera Aktiogavialis, Gryposuchus, Ikanogavialis, Piscogavialis, and Siquisiquesuchus.
